title: He didn’t want God.
paragraphs:
He didn’t want God.
He wanted what God could do.
And that difference exposed everything.
The story slips in quietly in Acts of the Apostles, but it doesn’t stay quiet for long. A man named Simon had already built a reputation. People listened when he spoke. They followed when he moved. Scripture says they called him “the great power of God.” He wasn’t just respected—he was feared, admired, elevated.
And he liked it that way.
Then something disrupted his world.
Philip came preaching Christ. Not tricks. Not illusions. Not manipulation. Jesus.
And people believed.
Demons fled. The sick were healed. Joy filled the city. Real power—not manufactured, not staged—real authority from heaven.
Simon saw it.
He watched crowds shift away from him… toward Jesus.
And for the first time, what he had wasn’t enough.
So he did what many do when they feel spiritual power slipping out of their control—he tried to attach himself to it.
Scripture says he “believed” and was baptized. On the outside, it looked right. He followed Philip. He stayed close.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
You can be near the move of God and still be far from the heart of God.
Then came the moment that exposed him completely.
When Peter the Apostle and John the Apostle arrived, they laid hands on believers, and the Holy Spirit came upon them.
And Simon saw it again.
Power.
Authority.
Impact.
Influence.
The kind of thing that makes people watch you.
And something rose up inside him—something old, something hidden, something he never surrendered.
Acts 8:18–19 says:
“When Simon saw that through laying on of the apostles’ hands the Holy Ghost was given, he offered them money, saying, ‘Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I lay hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost.’”
Read that again.
He didn’t ask for God.
He asked for power.
He didn’t desire transformation.
He desired control.
God saw it.
You knew.
That moment when your prayers were more about influence than surrender…
When you wanted the platform but not the cross…
When you wanted the gifts but not the Giver…
Simon just said it out loud.
But heaven had already judged it.
Peter didn’t comfort him.
He didn’t soften the truth.
He cut straight through the illusion.
Acts 8:20–21:
“Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money. Thou hast neither part nor lot in this matter: for thy heart is not right in the sight of God.”
Your heart is not right.
That’s the line most people never want to hear.
Because it means everything external can look aligned… while everything internal is still corrupt.
Simon wasn’t rejected because he lacked exposure.
He was rejected because he lacked surrender.
He wanted the authority of God without the lordship of Christ.
And that is still happening.
In pulpits.
On platforms.
In private prayers.
People chasing anointing without repentance.
Authority without obedience.
Spiritual visibility without spiritual death.
But Scripture is clear.
You cannot buy what only grace can give.
Ephesians 2:8–9:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
It’s a gift.
Not a transaction.
Not a strategy.
Not something you leverage.
Something you receive—with empty hands.
That’s where Simon failed.
He came with money.
God was looking for surrender.
And here’s the tension sitting on you right now…
Why do you want God?
Strip away the language. Strip away the appearance.
Is it Him?
Or is it what He can give you?
Because one leads to life.
The other leads to destruction dressed up as spirituality.
Jesus didn’t die so you could gain power.
He died so your sinful heart could be replaced.
Luke 9:23:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.”
Deny yourself.
That’s the part Simon never did.
That’s the part many still avoid.
But that’s where everything changes.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
Not surface-level inspiration—but truth that cuts, heals, and transforms.
Say it plainly: “God, fix my heart.”
Mean it.
Follow if you’re done playing with faith and ready to walk in it for real.
You’ll need it again when your motives start drifting.
